THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS

Montreal 


The Story of a Year 


IXTY-FIVE years ago the Young Men's Christian Associ- 
ation was founded in this City and for the first time on 
this Continent. With gratitude to God we assemble in 

this our Sixty-Fifth Annual Meeting to review the progress of 
the year and take a fresh outlook upon the future. We meet 
under the shadow of a great conflict which is testing the cour- 
age, strength, and resources of the Empire, and it is cause for 
thankfulness that under all the conditions prevailing, we are 
able to report another year of comparatively uninterrupted 
service in so many directions. 

It is now ten years since the growth of our local work made 
necessary the adoption of the Metropolitan form of organization 
as a preliminary step towards the establishment of Branches in 
the City, and this suggests a brief reference to several of the 
outstanding dates in our history. 

At the Fifth Annual Meeting, the Association occupied a 
suite of rooms at 205 Notre Dame Street, open each evening. 
The annual rental was £60. The membership roll contained 
205 members. The Committee after five years of work stated 
that they had “become more deeply convinced of the import- 
ance and value of the Young Men's Christian Associations, 
forming as they do, an agency of great power for reaching and 
bringing under the most favorable influences, the young men 
of the Community.” 

The Twenty-Fifth Annual Report, presented in 1876, 
found the Association in the Victoria Square Building, with a 
membership of 1,009. A widely extended programme, princi- 
pally of religious work, was reported upon, including mission 
work in public halls and schoolhouses in seven different locali- 
ties in the City. 

The Fiftieth Annual Report, in 1901, described the 
Jubilee of the Association held in the Dominion Square 
Building. The membership had reached ,2070. Work amongst 


Annual Report of the Board of Directors as Presented at the 
65th Annual Meeting of the Association, held in the Drummond St. 
Building, May 9th, 1916. 


Canadian soldiers in South Africa had been undertaken, the 
members having subscribed over $300.00, and about $3,000.00 
had been secured from outside sources and cabled to our Secret- 
aries in South Africa. The activities of the Association had be- 
come greatly enlarged and organized by departments upon the 
lines so familiar to us to-day. A map had been prepared by the 
Membership Committee showing the distribution of the mem- 
bers throughout the City and suggesting the expansion by 
Branches, which has since become an accomplished fact. 

When the Fifty-Fifth Annual Report was presented five 
years later, the membership had increased to 2,392 with the 
Dominion Square Building overcrowded. The Railroad Build- 
ing at Point St. Charles had been erected. Land for the exten- 
sion of the Dominion Square Building, and prospective sub- 
scriptions amounting to $40,000.00, had been secured. Branches 
in the East End and North End were being actively considered. 
As a preliminary step, the Metropolitan method of organization 
was adopted, and a Board of Management for the Central 
Building appointed, leaving the hands of the Directors free to 
undertake the outside extension. This was the year of Mr. 
Budge’s second visit to Australia, and of the death of Sir George 
Williams in England. 

In this connection a comparative statement showing the 
growth of the Associations in North America during the last 
fifteen years is of interest.

The direct activities of the Board find expression in the 
work of the following Committees :—Executive, Finance, Joint 
Fund, Property, Permanent Camp, Community, Military, and 
Work amongst Foreign Speaking Young Men. Sub-Committees 
of the Board are in charge of each of these undertakings, and 
careful attention has been given to them during the year. 

Current Finances—The Treasurer's Statement and the 
Report of the Joint Fund Committee will be laid before you 
this evening, giving complete information as to the securing 
and administration of our Current Funds. It is gratifying in 
the highest degree that during a war year, with so many special 
calls upon our members and the generosity of the public, we have 
been able to meet our obligations in the manner there described. 

Property.—The Buildings have been kept in repair by the 
Boards of Management of the respective Branches, and no 
major alterations have been made in them during the year. 

Building Fund.—In addition to the mortgage of $60,000.00 
upon the Buildings, the Building Fund indebtedness of $20,- 
221.10 over and above the mortgage was provided for by a note 
at the Merchants Bank of Canada early in the year. This note 
has been reduced by $1,486.69, and now amounts to $18,734.41. 
The Directors hope to make a further reduction at maturity. 
subscription of $1,000.00 towards the Building Fund of the 
Association has been received from Mr. H. E. Bydwell, same 
to be payable in ten annual instalments. 

Bequests.—The Directors have pleasure in mentioning the 
following bequests received during the year :-— 


Final payment from Orkney Estate.......-.-- $2,192.19 
First instalment from the legacy of the late Hugh

In addition, a bequest of $2,000.00 has been made to the 
Association by the Late George Hague for use in foreign lands 
under the direction of the International Committee. 

Permanent Camp Committee—The season of 1915 
was highly successful notwithstanding the war. The Boys’ 
Camp opened June 26th, closing August 25th. Mr. T. Hicks 
Miller, Physical Director at Westmount, had charge during 
July, and Mr. John McKinnon, Boys’ Work Secretary at Cen- 
tral, during August. Total attendance was 167 compared with 
Le the previous season. The attendance by Branches was as 

ollows -— 


Central 2...15.... 40 Railroad__........ 2 
North Branch... 41 East End......... I 
Westmount.......- 34 Visitors......-..--. 49 

—- 167 


The Men's Camp was open from July 9th to August 23rd, 
in charge of Mr. H. C. Patterson, Assistant Physical Director 
at Central. The total attendance for the summer was 141 com- 
pared with 160 the previous season. The Camp showed a sur- 
plus as follows:—Boys, $198.40; Men's, $208.57. This has been 
applied to the upkeep and improvement of the property. 


The Community Committee.—The Community Committee, 
first appointed four years ago, has continued its labors along the 
same general lines as last year. One principal objective has 
been the Public and High Schools of the City. The Board of 
School Commissioners granted the use of the William Lunn 
School three years ago as a community centre for evening work 
on behalf of children, young people, and parents living in that 
section of the City. The result of that experiment has led the 
Commissioners to adopt a policy of the wider use of school 
buildings under which, this year, twenty-one school buildings 
are now being used by thirty-nine organizations other than 
ourselves for welfare work. 

Talks and addresses have been arranged for in the various 
schools on subjects of interest to older boys. The attendance 
at these in the High School alone last year was 14,400, reaching 
1,800 students. Bible Study Groups have been promoted in 
the Montreal High and Technical Schools, the classes meeting 
at the Drummond Street Building. A field of effort of unusual 
significance has thus been opened up. 

Our Community Secretary co-operates widely with_or- 
ganizations working for boys in the City, including Boys’ Club 
work, Playground work, Sunday School Association the Daily 
Vacation Bible Schools, etc. 

The major portion of Mr. Bradford's time, however, has 
been given since December 1st to the East End Branch, where 
a new and important programme of activities adapted to the 
needs of that section of the City is being worked out. 


Work Amongst Foreigners.—This work, which heretofore 
has been carried on by the Community Committee, was trans- 
ferred in January to a new Committee under the Chairmanship 
of Mr. George E. Williams. This Committee has been in con- 
ference with representatives of the Churches, and has prepared 
a printed pamphlet giving results of a series of investigations 
showing the number of foreign people resident in Montreal, the 
location of the various colonies, the social and economic con- 
ditions under which they live, and the agencies at work on their 
behalf. Out of a population estimated at over 100,000, a liberal 
estimate places the total number reached by all present agencies 
at about 5,000. The official representatives of the various 


4 


churches have been communicated with and it is hoped to secure 
the co-operative action by the churches which will result in 
greater progress. 

Local Work for Soldiers —Upon the close of the Valcartier 
Camp and the return of the soldiers to the City in October last, 
space was kindly granted by General E. W. Wilson, O.C. of 4th 
Division, for a large recreation room at the Guy Street Barracks 
and work carried on there for the men of the 73rd Battalion 
with Mr. H. J. M. Fiske as Secretary in charge. Reading and 
writing materials, games, moving pictures, etc., were supplied 
and an attractive Song Service held each Sunday evening. In 
addition, Mr. Fiske visited the other Barracks in the City at 
regular intervals. The expense for the season was $960.05, 
towards which special subscriptions were received, amounting 
to $792.50. The balance will be assumed by the Canadian Na- 
tional Council. 

In addition to the above, the sum of $400.00 for Captain 
C. Gordon Armour’s work with the 24th Battalion was for- 
warded to the Canadian National Council. 

Mention should be made of the very large use of the Drum- 
mond Street Building by the various units in training in the 
City during the season. This has been appreciated in the high- 
est degree by both officers and men, and is a source of great 
pleasure and satisfaction to the Association. 

Another interesting feature was the organization of a Field 
Branch of the Association with the No. 9 Field Ambulance 
overseas in which several of our members co-operated. 


Work for Soldiers Abroad.—It will perhaps be fitting to 
mention in this Report that special effort on behalf of the sold- 
iers in Great Britain continues on the largest possible scale. 
The'Red Triangle’’ has become the emblem and title of this 
movement in khaki. The London correspondent of the “New 
York Sun” says that “the transmutation of the British Young 
Men's Christian Association under war conditions is remark- 
able. At first the Association was not wanted by the Military, 
but the effort was made and service rendered with such success 
that the Government began to grant facilities which have more 
than justified the extraordinary effort put forth. In addition, 
there are now one hundred and twenty-nine centres in France, 
several practically on the firing lines. 

“In Egypt twenty-seven centres have been established; in 
Malta, nine: while new headquarters are being erected in Corfu. 
In every Camp of soldiers undergoing training in England there 
are Association centres. 

“At the great railway terminals in London, Waterloo, 
Euston, Victoria, Paddington, and King’s Cross, there are large 


5 


Association quarters where soldiers arriving and departing to 
and from the front are cared for by the Association. These are 
never closed, night or day. 

‘The Island of Malta apparently is a great military head- 
quarters. Lord Methuen has assigned a suite of rooms in his 
palace for the administrative headquarters of the Association 
in that part of the world. 

“The ‘Red Triangle’ has come into its own, as has the 
Association on both sides of the ‘lines.’ 

The total expenditure of the British Associations up to 
November 30th last was $5,908,345.00, and further expenditure 
is proceeding at the rate of $3,000.00 daily to maintain work 
already undertaken in over one thousand centres. It is estim- 
ated that the total expenditure to date is about $7,000,000.00. 

The Work of Major Gerald W. Birks and the Military Service 
Fund.—Last summer our fellow member and Director of the 
Association, Mr. Gerald W. Birks, volunteered his services for 
work overseas on behalf of the Association. Our Canadian 
National Council at once appointed him as their Honorary 
Representative in England to organize and supervise the efforts 
of our Association Secretaries with the Canadian forces. The 
International Committee in New York, of which Mr. Birks is a 
member, also appointed him to act in a similar capacity for 
them in Europe. The wisdom of this action has been amply 
justified in the excellent results which have followed. The 
Board cannot speak too highly of the patriotic and unselfish 
service which Major Birks is rendering and which is a constant 
source of inspiration not only to our members but to the young 
manhood of the City. 

On October 1st last, the Board of Directors, members of 
the Boards of Management, and a representative group of 
members and friends of the Association took supper with Major 
Birks to wish him Godspeed on the eve of his departure. After 
six months’ service abroad, Major Birks returned on April 5th, 
accompanied by Rev. George Adam of London, England, to 
enlist our co-operation in raising the large sum of $300,000.00 
in Canada for Y.M.C.A. work amongst our Canadian soldiers 
at the front. A few days later the matter was placed before the 
Montreal public and, with the co-operation of about sixty of 
our members and friends, the splendid sum of over $82,000.00 
was raised in four days, which has since been increased by fur- 
ther gifts to $86,546.00 from Montreal. It is hoped that, with 
the co-operation of the other Canadian cities, the full amount 
needed will be realized. The addresses of the Rev. Mr. Adam 
were greatly enjoyed and he is to return for a series of meetings 
commencing May 15th in Emmanuel Church in this City. 


6 


Promotion of Prayer—During last summer the Executive 
Committee of the Association considered how prayer might be 
more widely promoted in the City and, after conference with 
interested friends, it was agreed to meet weekly on Wednesday 
at 12.30 for half an hour of intercession on behalf of the Empire, 
the progress of the war, our soldiers at the front; and the general 
progress of Christian work in the City. This meeting has con- 
tinued regularly since September with an encouraging attend- 
ance and deep interest. Several of our City ministers have 
united with the business men in this observance. 


The Week of Prayer for young men was observed in Nov- 
ember, and the Association united heartily with the Ministerial 
Association in the observance of the Week of Prayer in January, 
our Committee taking special responsibility for the noon meet- 
ing of business men held in St. Andrew's Church of Scotland. 


The Branches.—The work of our five Branches has already 
been reported upon in detail at their annual meetings held 
during the last ten days and it will only be necessary here to give 
briefly certain outstanding facts in which we are all interested. 


Activities have been well maintained notwithstanding 
unusual conditions. The constant enlistment of members has 
been felt throughout the year. 

The financial statements of the Branches are before you 
this evening in printed form. 

- The Central Branch closed the year on April 30th, with a 
total membership of 3,641 and a balance on hand of $10.37. 
During the year the following changes on the Staff took place: 

Mr. B. A. Prichard, who had served for a year as Member- 
ship Secretary, returned to the Y.M.C.A. at Buenos Ayres, 
South America. 

Mr. H. C. Patterson, Assistant Physical Director, volun- 
teered for Y.M.C.A. work overseas. 

Mr. Hay Finlay, Assistant Physical Director, enlisted with 
the 148th Battalion. 

Mr. J. S. Davis, Office Secretary, enlisted with the oth 
Field Ambulance Corps. 

Mr. John MacKinnon entered upon the position of Boys’ 
Work Secretary, August 1st last. 

Mr. W. A. MacLaren became Membership Secretary of 
the Branch December 1st. 

Mr. John Bradford, Community Secretary, served as Boys’ 
Work Secretary until December 1st. 

This Branch has always assumed special responsibility for 
the Paterson Fund and during the year, with the co-operation 
of the other Branches, $1,385.00 was raised for this purpose and 


7 


the usual sum remitted to the International Committee in New 
York, in support of the work of our representative, Mr. C. S. 
Paterson, in Calcutta. 

The North Branch closed the year on April 30th with a total 
membership of 1,061, and a balance on hand of $26.32. 

The Westmount Branch closed the year on April 30th, with 
a total membership of go9 and a balance on hand of $71.53. 
Mr. T. Hicks Miller, Physical Director of this Branch, volun- 
teered for Y.M.C.A. service overseas and was granted leave of 
absence by the Westmount Board from the end of April for this 
purpose. 

The Railroad Branch closed the year with a total member- 
ship of 486 and a balance on hand of $19.80. Mr. A. C. 
Johnston, Physical Director, resigned to enlist for overseas ser- 
vice with the 5th Pioneer Battalion. 

The East End Branch closed the year with a total member- 
ship of 200 and a balance of $164.36, part of which was 
subscribed with the expectation that it would be used for the 
expenses of the coming year. Mr. W. A. MacLaren acted as 
Secretary of this Branch until December 1st, when he became 
Membership Secretary at the Central Branch. Mr. John Brad- 
ford, Community Secretary, was asked by the Board to take 
charge of the work in the East End from December rst, giving 
half his time. 

Membership Campaign.—The outstanding feature of the 
year in the work of the Branches was the Campaign for new 
members to fill vacancies caused by enlistments for overseas 
service. All the Branches co-operated in this effort which took 
place during March 28th-31st. when 2,008 new members were 
secured. The Executive Committee of the Campaign consisted 
of Messrs. G. L. McCrae and W. C. Bradbury of the Central 
Branch: Messrs. F. B. Whittet and A. D. Charles of the West- 
mount Branch; Messrs J. S. Lang and S. W. Dugan, of the 
North Branch, with Mr. W. J. Holliday acting as Executive 
Secretary. To them and to every member of the special organ- 
ization our hearty thanks are due. 

At the opening function on Monday Evening, March 27th, 
when over three hundred members took supper in the large 
Central Building Gymnasium we were highly honored by the 
presence of His Royal Highness, the Duke of Connaught, 
whose gracious words of appreciation of the Association will 
long be remembered. 

Reference was made on this occasion to a former visit of 
His Royal Highness to the Association in 1870 when he was 
elected a Member of the Association. 

4 Honor Roll—The enlistment of so many of our members 
for the war has touched all our hearts in the deepest possible 


8 


manner. The Honor Rolls of our Branches now contain the 
names of members who have enlisted for overseas as follows —

In closing this report the Board would make the following 

recommendations :— 

1. That our Branches take special steps to meet in a more 
adequate way the great opportunity for personal 
Christian service amongst our more than 6,000 mem- 
bers in the City. 

>. That in view of the possibilities of co-operation be- 
tween the Branches, revealed by the Membership 
Campaign, full advantage be taken of this in prose- 
cuting other forms of activity. 

3. That from now on, special consideration be given to 
work for returned soldiers, especially with a view to 
the problems which will arise at the conclusion of the 
war and the opportunities that these will present to 
the Association. 

4. That the activities of the Association receive special 
study with a view to a thorough revision and enlarge- 
ment of plans in all departments. 


Respectfully submitted, 
J. W. KNOX, 


President. 
C. K. CALHOUN, 
General Secretary. 


MontrEAL, May oth, 1916.

16 


Speech of His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught 
at Opening Meeting of Y.M.C.A. Membership 
Campaign, on the 27th March, 1916 


“You are here tonight to start a rally to increase the membership of the 
Y.M.C. A,”’, said His Royal Highness. *‘Although I do not distinctly remember 
joining your Association in 1870, that may be forgiven—it is a long time ago. 
But for a great many years past I have witnessed the splendid work done by your 
Association. 


“In the many commands I have held in England and elsewhere, I have 
always received warm and generous assistance from the Y. M.C. A. They have 
especially always held out the right hand of fellowship to our soldiers, both reg- 
ulars and auxiliaries. - 1 can assure you that the good they have done in this way 
has been most marked and the feeling of good will and respect for your Association 
is well known in England as it is here. 


“T have seen a great deal of your Association's work in Canada,"’ proceeded 
His Royal Highness, “and I must congratulate you on the generous friendship 
and help always shown to those who required some assistance to keep them run- 
ning straight. 1 donot think you have ever failed in this work, and I know that 
your Association has done much to raise the tone and morality of the rising 
generation. 


“And, at the present moment, I know that your Association has warmly 
supported our military efforts in Canada to take an honorable part in the terrible 
struggle in which we are at present engaged. You have recognized that taking 
sO many men away from their civil avocations and families has placed them in a 
position where they are naturally more open to temptation than they would 
otherwise be. * 


‘You have done all possible to make them at home in your splendid institu- 
_tion. Your Association has done everything possible to help them, both in cities 
and camps, and I fully appreciate the immense amount of good you have done. 
I know that it is the universal feeling of the officers N.C.O.’s and men of the 
Canadian Overseas Forces that they are deeply indebted to the Y. M. C. A. for 
the splendid hospitality and kindness they have always met with at your hands. 


“This is a service of real value to the men and to the Dominion, and I hope 
that you will all do what you can to promote the interests of the Y. M. C. A., and 
continue the good work you are doing amongst our Canadian soldiers. We have 
every reason to be proud of the work they have done in this great war. We read 
day by day of the good work they are doing; of their pluck and intelligence, and 
of the splendid spirit of courage and devotion to duty that animates them. 


“Many of you who cannot go out yourselves are now in a position to show 
your sympathy by helping this movement which is so helpful both for the civilians 
and the soldiers. It has been a great pleasure to me to come amongst you this 
eyening, and I am sure you recognize that I speak from my heart in this. I. 
thoroughly recognize the good work you are doing and I urge you to continue it 
in every way. I hope my presence will show my sympathy with the objects of 
your meeting, and I can assure you I wish you every possible success.”’
